doc.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Advice, education and the evolution of jazz
title: Bar-walking, entertaining crowds, and Clifford Brown's integrity
summary: Golson recalls honking and walking bars with Tiny Grimes and catching Coltrane on a bar, and contrasts it with Clifford Brown, who never compromised.

bands.name: Chris Powell and the Five Blue Flames
Tiny Grimes and his Swinging Highlanders

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: But you used to walk the bars.
Oh, but I walked the bar. He might have turned over some drinks, but I never turned over a drink. I never tipped a drink.

Yes. Hey look – I caught my boy John Coltrane on the bar. When I opened that door and stepped in, and he was on that bar ready to turn where I was, he took his horn out of his mouth and looked at me and said, “Oh no,” and I fell out laughing.
Do you know where that tradition started?

I don’t know where it started. It didn’t start with the jazz artists, per se. It started with one of the entertainers. An entertainer’s plot is to do or to second-guess what the audience wants to hear. Yeah, I got involved in that. I did some crazy stuff when I was doing all that stuff. You do what you think is going to entertain them. It’s going to bring acclaim to what you’re doing. Yeah, what’s more ridiculous than getting up on the bar where the drinks are and start playing your low B-flats no matter what key you’re in, just honking. We call that honking and stepping. They’re applauding. Ain’t nothing happening. Stepping over those drinks.
You mentioned – like you said before – lowest common denominator.
That is what got the audience riled up.

I’m telling you. Clifford Brown was playing with a group like that, but when he played the solo, it was Clifford Brown. So it was an aberration to what was going on in that group. The people didn’t understand what he was playing from the jazz point of a jazz aficionado, but they knew what he was doing was great and unusual, and they accepted it, even though they didn’t under[stand] – because what he was – the things he was – this has got to be phenomenal, what this guy is doing. It had nothing to do with Chris Powell and the Five Blue Flames that were rocking it up and whatnot, and swaying from side to side. When he played, he played like Clifford Brown. It was like two different things. It’s incredible. He never compromised. I never heard him try to do anything else. He may be good at it. But every time he put that trumpet in his mouth, it was Clifford Brown, totally.
